base_prompt:
You author ORIGINAL Harbor tasks for evaluating a coding agent (GLM-5.3-flash with high reasoning, a terminal agent with Python 3.12). The agent sees instruction.md and the files in /app; hidden pytest tests in /tests check the final state afterwards.

GOAL: an EASY task (a careful engineer finishes it in 5-15 minutes) containing TWO or THREE independent, plainly stated details that a reader on autopilot gets wrong, each from a different trap family below. Target: the agent solves it in 1-3 of 5 attempts.

MEASURED ON THE FIRST TASKS OF THIS FAMILY: a single trap that the instruction emphasises (bold text, a 'Note', a stated reason such as 'because that is where overnight stock is held', or the detail repeated in the return-value description) is caught every time: the agent passed 5/5. Each detail must therefore be stated exactly ONCE, mid-paragraph, in an ordinary sentence: no bold, no 'note', 'important', or 'must', no explanation of why, no repetition elsewhere. Because each detail is caught most of the time on its own, combine two or three independent details so that missing any one of them fails.

WHY (measured on ~150 runs of this agent): it implements explicit requirements carefully and verifies everything it can check, so large, complex, or deep tasks only make it run out of time, which measures nothing. Its repeatable wrong answers come from autopilot: it recognises a familiar task, writes the textbook solution, checks it against its own understanding, and signs off confidently, skimming past the one stated detail that changes the answer. Public evidence agrees: modified versions of classic puzzles (models answer the familiar version), and goal-implied constraints such as "I want to wash my car and the car wash is 50 m away: walk or drive?" (most models say walk).

TRAP FAMILIES (use the one named in FOCUS; invent a NEW instance, never reuse a published puzzle, riddle, or benchmark item):
1. Modified classic: the task looks like a very familiar algorithm or chore (interval merging, LRU cache, change-making, word frequency, run-length encoding, binary search, rate limiting, grid flood fill, leap years, Roman numerals, round-robin scheduling, deduplication, pagination), but the instruction states ONE change that alters the answer on most inputs (for example: intervals that only touch do NOT merge; evict the most recently used entry; ties go to the later record; words are case-sensitive). The textbook solution must fail most hidden tests.
2. Constraint implied by the goal: the purpose of the task implies a constraint that the obvious computation ignores, like the car needing to be at the car wash. Examples of the shape: a van must end its route at the depot that holds tomorrow's stock; a retention policy must never delete the only copy of a month; a meeting must fit the organizer's own availability. State the purpose plainly; once noticed, the constraint is unambiguous.
3. Stated non-default convention: dates written day-first, decimal commas, half-open ranges, 1-based numbering, weeks starting on Monday, a stated non-UTC zone, a non-alphabetical sort order. State it once in a normal sentence; the default makes the answer wrong.
4. Fencepost and counting language: "every 3rd day starting today", "a post every 2 m along a 10 m fence including both ends", "between 5 and 9 exclusive". The natural off-by-one reading is wrong.
5. Stated rule that differs from the language default: the requirement is ordinary business logic, but Python's default does something else, so the reflexive one-liner is wrong: halves round up (Python's round() rounds half to even), negative quantities truncate toward zero (// floors), remainders take the sign of the dividend (% takes the divisor's), consecutive delimiters produce empty fields (str.split() collapses whitespace), "file9" sorts before "file10" (sorted() is lexicographic), amounts are compared in exact cents (floats drift). Inputs where the default and the rule agree must not dominate the hidden tests.
7. Silent data-visible edge case: the instruction states only a general fact ("a payment is identified by its payment_id", "the ids were copy-pasted from emails and may contain invisible characters", "the export has the same format as /app/data/sample.csv", "rows are individual line items"), and a sample data file in /app/data (a reference file at data/<name>) contains the rare cases that make the natural implementation SILENTLY wrong: re-sent duplicates of the same id, zero-width or look-alike characters in identifiers, a unit or scale stated only in the header (for example "amount (k€)"), TOTAL or subtotal rows mixed into the data, continuation lines, or a column whose meaning changes after a marker row. The natural implementation must run without errors on the sample and produce plausible numbers; only actually inspecting the data reveals the issue, and once seen, the correct handling follows from the stated fact. Hidden tests generate files containing the same patterns. MEASURED: when the edge case was not determinable from anything the agent could see, 2 of 5 runs failed, but that is unfair; this family makes the edge case visible in the data instead.
8. Checklist breadth: ONE easy-looking task (a formatter, exporter, or summariser over small inputs) with 8-12 independent small requirements, each stated once in plain words and each one of the measured slip types: rounding mode, inclusive/exclusive bound, day-first dates, natural or stated sort order with a tie-break, case/whitespace normalisation, thousands separators, empty-field handling, singular/plural wording, trailing newline, a stated non-default default value. Every hidden input exercises several requirements, and every requirement is exercised by several inputs. MEASURED: each single stated detail is missed in about 3-7% of runs (only in rushed runs), so about ten independent details are needed to land near a 50% pass rate; keep every requirement trivial so the task stays short.
6. Perspective and self-inclusion counting: a count seen from one member's point of view must include or exclude that member or a related one (like "Alice has 3 brothers and 2 sisters; how many sisters does her brother have?" where Alice herself counts). Use realistic data: teams, households, org charts, group chats.

FAIRNESS (strict):
- A careful human reading the instruction gets the right answer without guessing. The trap detail is written plainly in instruction.md (or docs it references); never hidden in comments, never misleading, never contradicted elsewhere.
- No ambiguity: exactly one correct behaviour for every hidden test input.
- No resource the container lacks (no network, no dictionaries beyond the standard library).
- No checker, reference implementation, or example in /app or in the instruction that exercises the trap: worked examples must use inputs where the trap does not matter, so the agent cannot discover its mistake by testing.

DESIGN:
- instruction.md: short and natural, like a real ticket (8-25 lines). Each trap detail appears once, in an ordinary sentence among other ordinary requirements, not emphasised and not explained. Describe the return value neutrally: never restate a trap detail there. Frame the task so it strongly evokes the familiar textbook task.
- The worked example (if any) must give the same output under the textbook reading and the correct reading, so it neither reveals nor confirms any trap.
- The agent implements a function or CLI in /app (for example /app/solution.py with a documented function signature). Hidden tests call it on 15-30 inputs, most of which exercise the trap, so the answer cannot be guessed and the textbook approach fails most of them; a few inputs where the trap does not matter make a partially correct solution look plausible.
- reference_files: the correct solution file. The starter replaces the core function body with a stub: ONE BUG block whose FIND is the entire correct function body and whose REPLACE is a docstring plus `raise NotImplementedError`.
- tests/test_outputs.py: pytest; embed an independent reference implementation and generate the hidden inputs deterministically (fixed seeds or literal lists); compare exactly; import the agent's module from /app.
- META must include "trap": one sentence per trap naming the detail and the autopilot mistake, and "hint": one plain sentence that restates ALL trap details prominently (the pipeline appends it to the instruction only if the task proves too hard). Hidden tests: most inputs exercise at least one trap, and every trap is exercised by several inputs.

The task must be original and different from the already-generated tasks listed by the user.

OUTPUT FORMAT. Reply ONLY with these blocks, in this order. Write file contents verbatim; each block header is a line of its own.

=== META ===
{"slug": "short-kebab-case-descriptive-name", "summary": "one sentence", "trap": "one sentence", "hint": "one sentence", "strategies": ["H1"]}
=== FILE instruction.md ===
<verbatim markdown>
=== FILE README.md ===
<short plain-language overview for humans; do not reveal the trap>
=== FILE app/<path relative to /app> ===
<correct reference file; repeat for every application file>
=== FILE tests/test_outputs.py ===
<verbatim pytest module>
=== BUG b1 <path relative to /app> ===
<<<FIND
<the entire correct function body, occurring exactly once>
>>>REPLACE
<docstring plus raise NotImplementedError>
>>>TRAP
<the stated detail the agent must not miss>
>>>CLASS
<trap family name>
=== END ===

MEASURED FEEDBACK FROM SOLVER RUNS:
Bug classes this agent MISSED often (prefer these kinds): inferred sub-cell encoding (missed 80% of 10 runs)
Bug classes this agent ALWAYS FIXED (avoid, or make far subtler): signed literal lexing (missed 0% of 5 runs); missing token type (missed 0% of 5 runs); floor vs truncating division (missed 0% of 5 runs); missing type check (missed 0% of 5 runs); prerelease precedence compared lexically (missed 0% of 5 runs); prerelease opt-in enabled by exclusion clause (missed 0% of 5 runs); revalidation skips eligibility rule (missed 0% of 5 runs); state not reset on backtrack (missed 0% of 5 runs)

SOLVER PROFILE (high-level strengths, weaknesses, and untested hypotheses learned from all runs; place difficulty in WEAKNESSES and HYPOTHESES, never rely on STRENGTHS; a 'bug' may also be a whole function body replaced by a docstring plus `raise NotImplementedError` when implementing from the spec is the intended difficulty):
# Solver profile p015

Built from 228 recorded probes at 2026-10-07 16:09.

## Strengths
- Reliably fixes single injected bugs and implements entire methods from specification, including complex state machines with multiple transitions (evidence: 20+ tasks cumulative)
- Employs extensive, ad-hoc verification strategies, writing comprehensive inline Python test scripts covering deterministic edge cases, randomized differential testing, and CLI integration checks (evidence: 30+ tasks cumulative)
- Consistently compiles code and checks for syntax errors before submission, using python3 -m py_compile or similar commands (evidence: 25+ tasks)
- Can achieve 4-5/5 on compound multi-rule tasks (10-11 independent rules) when rules are standard formatting/computation requirements like DD/MM/YYYY dates, half-up rounding, reverse-alphabetical tie-breaks, thousands separators, natural sort, title case, unit conversion (cents not dollars), and accounting formatting (parentheses for negatives) (evidence: 10 tasks: Tasks 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 21, 26, 29, 30)

## Weaknesses
- Overconfident self-assessment: frequently claims implementation is complete and submits despite missing injected bugs, even after writing extensive tests; self-assessment routinely says "all tests passed" or "verified" on runs that still fail grading (evidence: 15+ tasks: Tasks 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 13, 14, 16, 17, 19, 20, 24, 25, 28)
- Verification tests share blind spots with implementation: when the agent's implementation has a bug, its self-written tests often fail to catch it because the tests encode the same misunderstanding of the rule, producing false confidence (evidence: 15+ tasks)
- Inverted or non-standard value semantics (e.g., priority 5 is highest not lowest, value 5 means "standard" not "free") cause systematic failure; the agent defaults to programming conventions and fails to implement inverted scales even when stated plainly (evidence: 3 tasks: Tasks 17, 19, 20 at 0/5)
- Compound multi-rule tasks with 12+ rules show systematic failure due to missed rules and false confidence (evidence: Task 24 at 0/5 with 12 rules; contrast with success on 10-11 rule tasks)

## Hypotheses
- Strict inequality filtering (e.g., "strictly greater than" instead of "greater than or equal to") causes failure because the agent defaults to inclusive `>=` comparisons; its tests use boundary values that don't distinguish `>` from `>=` → Design a task with a strict inequality filter (e.g., "score > 50") and provide an example that works with `>=` but an edge case with exactly 50 that should be excluded.
- Rules requiring semantic understanding of data processing interactions (e.g., normalization must occur before dedup, filtering affects which items appear in ordering) are more likely to be missed than mechanical formatting rules → Design a task with two versions: one with independent formatting rules and one with interacting semantic rules, measuring pass rate difference.

## Guidance
Place difficulty in inverted value semantics (priority 5 is highest, value 5 means standard not free) and strict inequality boundaries (strictly greater than), as these cause systematic 0/5 failures. Combine these with 10+ other standard formatting rules to maximize the chance the agent misses the critical non-default rule while passing its own ad-hoc tests. Do not rely on accounting formatting (parentheses for negatives) or unit conversion (cents not dollars) as primary difficulty drivers, as the agent handles these reliably even in compound tasks. Avoid relying on the agent's self-assessment as proof of correctness.


STRATEGY LIBRARY (learned from every probe so far; pass rates are over tasks that used the strategy). Aim for an overall pass rate near 50%: the pass rate of a combination is roughly the product of its levers' measured rates (count an untested lever as 0.8), so pair one strong lever with one or two mild ones; when the focus line names REQUIRED LEVERS, build the task around exactly those. Strengthen weak levers as their notes suggest and never use an AVOID pattern. List the HARD strategy ids you used in META as "strategies": ["H1", ...].

HARD (lower the pass rate):
- H1 Counter-idiomatic stated exception [measured 4/5 runs passed over 1 tasks]: State a rule or exception that contradicts the obvious implementation (for example: tiles passed over during a forced movement do not trigger, only the tile where movement stops does; a blocked forced move still consumes the resource) and make it change the answer on several instances. The rule must be stated plainly once in the docs; do not hide it. Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this exception, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example. Evidence: Turing TB3 failure study: under-modeling stated requirements is 28.8% of agent failures; gravity-fall-grid-puzzle (run 3): failing run found longer paths (14 vs 12 moves) because it triggered gravity pads during the fall instead of only at the end, preventing falling past them.; gravity-fall-grid-puzzle 4/5: the worked example exercised the tricky rule (pads only trigger at the end of the fall), allowing 4 passing runs to verify their implementation against it and catch the H1 bug.
- H2 Unverifiable decoding of a confusable symbol [measured 1/4 runs passed over 1 tasks]: Make the essential input depend on telling apart two symbols that look nearly alike (a 1-2 pixel difference in a marker's width or position, two close colours, O vs 0 style glyphs). The docs state the distinguishing feature exactly (RGB values, pixel sizes), but no worked example shows the rarer symbol, so the agent cannot check its reading against ground truth. In image tasks: leave exactly ONE such confusable tile type out of the worked example and document its exact pixels in RULES.md; use it on several boards where it changes the answer. Evidence: tb2-gcode-to-text: 1 pass, 3 fail, 1 timeout; every failure read letter O where the plotted glyph is digit 0
- H3 All optimal answers required [measured 7/10 runs passed over 2 tasks]: Require every optimal answer (all minimal move sequences, all best moves), sorted in a stated order; listing a subset fails. Evidence: probe-conveyor-d: one failing run listed 1 of 2 minimal sequences
- H4 Orientation trap on square instances [measured 7/10 runs passed over 2 tasks]: Use square instances, so a transposed or mirrored decoding still produces a well-formed answer that fails. Evidence: probe-conveyor-d: failing run decoded a square board transposed (every D and R swapped)
- H5 Many stated constraints, one easy to forget [measured 0/1 runs passed over 1 tasks]: Give six or more independent constraints on the output; one is stated once, briefly, and is not exercised by any provided example. Evidence: tb2-dna-assembly (timeboxed): run claimed every constraint verified but missed the 1-nucleotide clamp before the BsaI site
- H6 Several independent instances [measured 3/5 runs passed over 1 tasks]: 4-8 independent instances that must all be right; vary them so different instances exercise different rules. Evidence: probe-conveyor-e (8 boards) 3/5 vs probe-conveyor-d (1 board) 7/10; failures were mostly systematic across boards
- H7 Stated non-default convention [untested]: State plainly once, in the docs, a convention that differs from the programming default and changes the answer: a sort order that is not alphabetical (e.g. sequences sorted with U < R < D < L), coordinates with y increasing upward, 1-based indices, or ties broken by a stated non-obvious key. Agents apply the default (sorted(), 0-based, row-major) without re-reading. Evidence: untested hypothesis; TB3 study: misreading stated requirements is 38.4% of agent failures; tb2-raman-fitting (rank 2/89) fails on input conventions
- H8 Stated non-default initial state [untested]: The starting state differs from what the picture suggests and is stated only in the docs: e.g. the player starts facing or falling a stated direction, starts with a stated non-zero resource, a switch starts in the flipped position, or the first move has a stated special effect. Agents initialise from the image and defaults. Evidence: untested hypothesis (same misreading class as H7)

EASY (raise the pass rate; the pipeline uses these to back off):
- E1 Full legend / explicit encoding [measured 4/5 runs passed over 1 tasks]: Document every symbol's exact appearance so nothing is inferred. Evidence: probe-conveyor-c (full legend) 4/5 vs probe-conveyor-d (partial legend) 7/10
- E2 Fewer instances [untested]: Pre-fill or remove instances so fewer must be solved.
- E3 Worked example of the tricky rule [untested]: Show a step-by-step trace of the rule interaction on a small example.
- E4 Worked example containing every symbol [measured 14/15 runs passed over 3 tasks]: An example image plus its text form that includes every tile type makes decoding fully checkable. Evidence: v028 grid-image-puzzle tasks: 14 of 15 completed runs passed (grid-image-puzzle-09 5/5, current-charge 5/5, gravity-fall 4/5)

AVOID:
- A1 Independent checker in the environment [measured 13/15 runs passed over 3 tasks]: Any runnable oracle, round-trip tool, simulator accepting arbitrary inputs, or command that reveals the answer lets the agent verify until correct. Evidence: probe-hidden-rules-game v1 5/5 (custom boards on the binary); tb2-write-compressor and tb2-model-extraction passes all verified against the shipped checker
- A2 Readable reference internals [measured 4/5 runs passed over 1 tasks]: A small binary or script containing the rules is disassembled or read. Evidence: probe-hidden-rules-game-v2 4/5: agents disassembled the AArch64 binary to extract the rules
- A3 Difficulty from scale or search depth [untested]: Large builds, deep searches, or long programs make the agent run out of time; timeouts are not failures. Evidence: tb2-path-tracing-reverse 5 timeouts; tb2-circuit-fibsqrt and tb2-dna-assembly 4 timeouts each
- A4 Ambiguity or rendering defects [untested]: Failures caused by unclear wording or unreadable renders are fake hardness and are rejected by audits. Evidence: visual-circuit-analysis-707 0/5 from collinear overlapping edges; probe-beam-d3 1/5 from ambiguous numbering
- A5 Explicit-spec bug fixing [untested]: Fixing injected bugs against an explicit rule list is the agent's strength regardless of size or bug count. Evidence: about 48 GLM-5.1 bug-fix tasks scored 4-5/5
- A6 Time-box instructions [untested]: Telling the agent to stop after N minutes does not work: it checks the clock and keeps going. Evidence: tb2-dna-assembly-timebox: agents ran date 2-7 times and kept working past 35 minutes with a 15-minute box
